title: The one controller
theme: The one controller, the inner self of all beings, who makes one form many: those wise ones who see him abiding in themselves have eternal happiness, and not others.

words.role: subject (with vaśī and sarvabhūtāntarātmā) of the relative clause

words.meaning: controller, one who has all in his power
the inner self of all beings

words.context: Śaṅkara: manifest in the space of the heart in one’s own body, in the intellect, «स्वशरीरहृदयाकाशे बुद्धौ चैतन्याकारेणाभिव्यक्तमित्येतत्»
Śaṅkara: experience directly, following the teacher and scripture, «आचार्यागमोपदेशमनु साक्षादनुभवन्ति»

words.role: subject of the verbless clause (asti understood)
negates the clause for the others

sandhi.rule: -aḥ becomes -o before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).
Final m stays before a vowel and is joined to it.
After e at the end of a word an initial a is merged into it, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति); the avagraha marks it.
Visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

sandhi_exceptions.note: sarvabhūtāntarātmā ekam: ā before e is not fused. The words end the first pāda and begin the second, and both are counted (11 + 11); fused (sarvabhūtāntarātmaikam) the half-line would have 21. Every witness keeps the vowels apart.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa (with a karmadhāraya in each member)
samasa.vigraha: सर्वाणि भूतानि सर्वभूतानि, अन्तरः आत्मा अन्तरात्मा, सर्वभूतानाम् अन्तरात्मा
samasa.meaning: the inner self of all beings

morphology.note: vaśin, a possessive in -in from vaśa, ‘will, control’: ‘having control’. Raṅgarāmānuja: «सोऽस्यास्तीति वशी».
An adverb in -dhā, ‘in many ways’, from bahu.

translation.literal: The one controller, the inner self of all beings, who makes one form manifold — the wise who perceive him abiding in [their] self, theirs [is] everlasting happiness, not of others.
translation.readable: There is one who rules all, the self within every being, who makes the one form many. The wise who see him dwelling within themselves have lasting happiness; others do not.

syntax: The first line is a string of nominatives (ekaḥ vaśī sarvabhūtāntarātmā) closed by a relative clause, yaḥ … karoti. They are taken up by tam in the second line, object of the relative clause ye … anupaśyanti dhīrāḥ, whose correlative teṣām introduces a verbless clause: ‘theirs is lasting happiness’. na itareṣām denies it to the rest.

ambiguities.topic: What is the ‘one form’ made many?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: his own one, uniform self of pure consciousness, made manifold through the adjuncts of name and form, «एकमेव सदैकरसमात्मानं विशुद्धविज्ञानघनरूपं नामरूपाद्यशुद्धोपाधिभेदवशेन बहुधा अनेकप्रकारेण यः करोति». Raṅgarāmānuja reads ‘one seed’ (ekaṃ bījam) in the mūla printed with his comment, and explains it as the undivided primal matter, tamas, made into the many-formed world, «स्वेन एकीभूताविभागावस्थं तमोलक्षणं बीजम्».
Śaṅkara: the whole world is in his power. Raṅgarāmānuja gives that sense and also ‘controlled by his devotees’, «भक्तवश्यः इति वा अर्थः».

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Two lines of 22 syllables (11 + 11), counting sarvabhūtāntarātmā and ekam apart, as all witnesses write them.

beginner: Death now names the self within all beings as the one ruler of everything. He makes one thing into many, as one lump of clay becomes many pots. The wise who look within and find him there have a happiness that does not fade, and others do not. Śaṅkara says the one self only appears as many because of names and forms laid over it, and the joy found is the self’s own bliss. Raṅgarāmānuja, whose copy reads ‘one seed’, says God turns the one unformed seed of matter into the whole world, and that those who see him as their inner ruler gain freedom. Madhva says the souls that look like God’s many forms are utterly different from him, because they depend on him. All three agree that the happiness comes from seeing him within.
analogy: One composer’s single theme heard in a hundred variations: each variation is different, the theme is one.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The one controller, the inner self of all beings, makes one form many; lasting happiness belongs to the wise who see him abiding within themselves, and to no one else.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: one self made many by adjuncts
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The supreme Lord is all-pervading and independent, one, with none equal or greater, «स हि परमेश्वरः सर्वगतः स्वतन्त्रः एकः, न तत्समोऽभ्यधिको वान्योऽस्ति»; the whole world is in his power. He makes his own one self many through adjuncts of name and form. He abides in the self as a face abides in a mirror, «आदर्शस्थं मुखमिति यद्वत्», not as a body is held in a place. Those who turn from outward things and see him have lasting happiness, the bliss of the self, «शाश्वतं नित्यं सुखम् आत्मानन्दलक्षणं भवति»; others do not, though it is their own self, because ignorance stands between, «नेतरेषां बाह्यासक्तबुद्धीनामविवेकिनां स्वात्मभूतमपि, अविद्याव्यवधानात्».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the one seed and the inner ruler
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He reads ekaṃ bījam: the one seed, primal matter in its undivided state, «स्वेन एकीभूताविभागावस्थं तमोलक्षणं बीजम्», which the Lord makes into the many-formed world of mahat and the rest, «महदादिबहुविधप्रपञ्चरूपेण». He cites the Subāla for the seed becoming one with the god, «तमः परे देव एकी भवति», as cited by him. Those who see him as their own inner ruler, «स्वान्तर्यामिणं ये पश्यन्ति, तेषामेव मुक्तिरित्यर्थः».

commentary.q: Madhva: the soul is utterly other
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: His comment after this mantra cites a verse he attributes to the Mahākaurma: the soul shows consciousness, Hari is the supreme conscious one, «चेतनाभासको जीवः परमश्चेतनो हरिः», and being independent he is not touched by fault, «स्वतन्त्रत्वात् स्वतन्त्रो हि नैव दोषेण लिप्यते» (cited by Madhva). Then: he alone is the inner self of all beings, «स एक एव सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा»; the soul called his counterpart came to be, «तस्य रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपाख्यो जीवो बभूव», and it is utterly different from the supreme Self, being dependent, «बहिश्चासौ परमात्मनो नितरां भिन्नः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The mūla printed with Raṅgarāmānuja’s comment, and his own gloss, read bījam, ‘seed’, where all our witnesses read rūpam, ‘form’. His gloss shows he commented on bījam; no witness of this edition has it.

advaita.text: The Lord makes his own one self many through name and form; seeing him within is the self’s own bliss, kept from others by ignorance, «अविद्याव्यवधानात्».

visistadvaita.text: The Lord turns the one seed of primal matter into the world; those who see him as their inner ruler are freed, «स्वान्तर्यामिणं ये पश्यन्ति, तेषामेव मुक्तिरित्यर्थः».

dvaita.text: The soul, called the Lord’s counterpart, is utterly different from him because it depends on him: «बहिश्चासौ परमात्मनो नितरां भिन्नः».

schools.disagreement: The ‘one form made many’ is the one self under adjuncts (Śaṅkara), or primal matter made into the world, on the reading ‘one seed’ (Raṅgarāmānuja); Madhva’s comment turns to the souls as the Lord’s dependent counterparts. All three tie lasting happiness to seeing him within.

parallels.quote: यः सर्वाणि भूतान्यन्तरो यमयत्येष त आत्मान्तर्याम्यमृत
parallels.note: The inner controller who governs all beings from within: the ‘controller, inner self of all beings’ of this verse.

parallels.quote: एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बहिश्च
parallels.note: The one inner self of all beings, first named in the fire image.

contemporary.text: Many traditions locate lasting contentment inward rather than in what changes outside. The verse adds a condition, seeing, not just believing. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: What kind of happiness have you known that did not depend on anything outside you?
reflect.deeper: rūpam or bījam: how does one word change what ‘making one many’ means?
reflect.practice: For a few minutes, look for what is steady beneath your changing thoughts, without naming it.

flags.note: The mūla printed with Raṅgarāmānuja’s comment reads ekaṃ bījam, and he comments on bījam; all witnesses of this edition read ekaṃ rūpam. corrections.json records only spacing differences (V) for this mantra.
What is made many: the self under adjuncts (Śaṅkara), the seed of primal matter (Raṅgarāmānuja); Madhva’s comment speaks of the souls as dependent counterparts.

Madhva’s comment after this mantra opens with a verse on the Lord’s freedom from fault (the theme of 2.2.11), attributed by him to the Mahākaurma, and then glosses the words sarvabhūtāntarātmā and rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo bahiś ca, which belong to 2.2.9–10; only his words on the inner self and the soul are read here as bearing on 2.2.12.
